packet_structure.blank_duplex_backs: Even-numbered scan pages are blank backs and were not treated as missing evidence.

grading_basis: Formative engineering-design evidence: criteria/constraints, research/planning, testing, iteration, and claim-evidence-reasoning. Writing mechanics were not scored.

students.name: Natalie
students.rating_rationale: Your design thinking stays consistent from research through testing: you predicted that a wide base would help, tested the tower, and connected success to that feature. Next, make the reasoning more scientific by explaining how the wide base reduces tipping and by citing the specific trial result in the reasoning sentence.
students.highest_leverage_need: Strengthen the reasoning link between measured evidence and why the design feature caused greater stability.

students.name: Leah
students.rating_rationale: You have useful stability ideas and you collected two trial results, but the final explanation does not yet show a clear claim-evidence-reasoning chain. Use the numbers from the data table, then explain how a design feature such as a better base or lower center of gravity caused the tower to resist tipping.
students.highest_leverage_need: Build a complete CER that cites numerical test evidence and explains the cause of stability.

students.name: Charlie
students.rating_rationale: You show a strong engineering process: you considered stability features, built and tested several versions, and recorded measurable results. The next step is to make your redesign stay inside the constraints and to explain how a specific structural feature caused the successful trial to stand.
students.highest_leverage_need: Use test evidence to justify an improvement that still obeys all material constraints.

students.name: Dylan
students.rating_rationale: You have strong design ideas and your data shows a large improvement from one successful tower to the next. To make the evidence convincing, cite the 51 cm and 89 cm results and explain how the base or triangular bracing changed the tower's resistance to tipping.
students.highest_leverage_need: Turn the successful test data into specific evidence and causal reasoning about the base structure.

strengths: All four students identified at least one plausible stability feature such as a wide base, lower center of gravity, stronger bottom support, or triangular structure.
All four recorded test results and distinguished whether a tower met the 10-second free-standing requirement.
Students generally used testing to suggest a next design change rather than treating the first build as final.
needs: CER evidence is often qualitative when numerical height and stand-time data are available.
Reasoning frequently names a feature ('wide base,' 'sturdy,' 'stable bottom') without explaining the cause-and-effect mechanism that reduces tipping.
Redesign ideas should be checked explicitly against the fixed material constraints before being accepted.
class_findings.highest_leverage_target: Move from 'what feature helped' to 'what the data shows and why that feature caused greater stability.'

notes: No separate numeric, percentage, point, or letter grade was added.
All Set 1 answers were independently checked once before rendering.
No graph or nontrivial diagram asset was required for this evidence set.
